The eleven ratings for Indus Holding
INDUS Holding AG · INH-DE · Xetra

The decision for Richard

Do not own the shares nowAt the fair multiple of 8.9x, the 18-month total return is about zero, and the skew is negative into the cut to FY27 estimates that I expect in two steps between November 2026 and March 2027.
Do not short into 12 NovemberStrong share-price momentum and a Q3 2026 report that is more likely to be good than bad make a short position before 12 November a poor bet.
Buy at EUR 24 to 30, on three signalsBuy when the share price reaches EUR 24 to 30 and three signals are visible together: the working-capital release reducing net debt, acquisitions being announced again, and the initial FY27 guidance range set and absorbed by the market.

INDUS is booking the largest profit in its history from a temporary tungsten windfall, and the share price has already paid for that profit. INDUS is a German industrial holding company that owns 43 small companies permanently. Its normal economics do not compound: an adjusted EBITA margin of 8 to 10%, a post-tax return on capital employed (ROCE) of about 8.5%, a cash conversion cycle of about 200 days and organic growth of 2 to 4% a year over the cycle. In 2026 one subsidiary, BETEK (about 16% of group sales), captured a scarcity premium on tungsten that Chinese export policy created, and INDUS carried the industry's inventory on its own balance sheet to do it. Every source, including management, says the premium is temporary.

The market has priced the windfall as if it were durable. The shares are up 69% in twelve months to a multiple at the top of their own five-year range, 86% of the sell-side rate them Buy, and estimates are at their highs. The dashboard's phase rule reads the stock as "Reinforcing" and gives the model a guideline multiple of 14.26x, which produces a modelled 18-month return of +99.5%.

My view is that INDUS is at the end of its reinforcing phase, not in the middle of it. In FY27 earnings fall by about a third while free cash flow rises from about zero to about EUR 180m. Consensus will be cut in two steps between November 2026 and March 2027. The fair multiple is the company's own ten-year median of about 8.9x on brokers'-basis earnings, which gives an 18-month total return of about zero and a three-year return in the high twenties.

The opportunity is a dated route to a clean long. Which outcome is unfolding will be visible by March 2027. The enterprise value is far more stable than the equity story, because the tungsten price that cuts earnings also releases cash. A de-rating of the shares into the mid-to-high twenties while the balance sheet visibly repairs is the configuration in which INDUS becomes a clean long.

Basis of the earnings figures: every EPS figure compared with consensus or multiplied by a valuation multiple is on the brokers' basis (after amortisation of acquired intangibles from purchase price allocation, PPA, and before one-off items). End note 1 reconciles the bases.

Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

1

INDUS's headline profit cycle and its underlying volume cycle are out of phase, and the headline cycle turns down first. The FY26 peak in reported revenue and profit is made of price. Adjusted EBITA rises by about EUR 90m, from EUR 147.8m in FY25 to EUR 238.7m in FY26 (the model, at the guidance midpoint), and about EUR 84m of that increase is Materials Solutions. Within Materials Solutions, the gain came from BETEK passing a tungsten feedstock price that tripled, and then tripled again, through to customers who were short of supply. The volume cycle in the other two-thirds of the group is positive for the first time in three years (organic growth of 3% in Engineering and 4% in Infrastructure in H1 2026), but it is shallow and still waits for a German capex and construction recovery that rising interest rates keep postponing. From Q4 2026 the group headline falls while the underlying volume slowly improves: group numbers will show deterioration, and segment numbers will show a normalisation with a modest recovery underneath.

2

In FY27 INDUS's earnings and cash flow move in opposite directions, and the market has modelled only the fall in earnings. On the model, FY27 adjusted EBITA falls 27% to EUR 174m and brokers'-basis EPS falls 34% to EUR 3.22. At the same time, free cash flow before acquisitions and dividends rises from about zero to about EUR 182m, because EUR 80m or more of working capital is released as the tungsten price falls. Net financial debt falls from about EUR 657m to EUR 571m, and the equity ratio reaches the company's 40% target during 2027. Consensus FY27 free cash flow of EUR 131m contains essentially no working-capital release: consensus operating cash flow of EUR 206m is what EBITDA of EUR 292m leaves after tax and interest, with no room for a release. The cash surprise is therefore as large as the earnings disappointment, but the market will not credit the cash until it has taken the earnings cut.

3

Consensus FY27 EPS of EUR 3.94 is stale, and the cut to it has a timetable. Five of the seven brokers last updated in July or August, on the strength of the FY26 guidance raise. The two brokers that updated after the company's October conference (NuWays at EUR 3.63 and Metzler at EUR 3.65) sit 8% below the median, and my EUR 3.22 sits 18% below it. I expect the median to move toward the updated pair at the 12 November report, and toward the company's initial FY27 guidance range in March 2027, which I expect at adjusted EBITA of EUR 160 to 195m (an 8 to 10% margin). Breadth of revisions, target prices and the revision-momentum score are all at their highs, and the one-month revision is already zero. For a long position, this is the wrong end of the estimate cycle.

4

The share price has already paid the re-rating, and the shares now trade on the company's own next three reports. The 24-month-forward P/E is 8.5x on FactSet's five-year series (89th percentile; median 6.7x) and 9.5x on the dashboard's ten-year series (median 8.9x). The re-rating from about 6.7x a year ago happened on a one-off level of earnings. The share's daily variance is 84% idiosyncratic against its peer basket, so the sector did not push the shares up and will not cushion them on the way down.

5

The guideline fair multiple of 14.26x is an artefact of the phase rule, and the model's +99.5% return should not be carried. The 90th-percentile multiple belongs to 2017 and 2018, when INDUS compounded at double-digit margins with positive organic growth and zero interest rates. Applying that multiple to a company whose earnings fall 30% inside the return window double-counts, and applying it to pre-PPA EPS, which is about 31% above the basis on which the multiple's history was measured, adds a second error. At the ten-year median of 8.9x on brokers'-basis 24-month-forward EPS of about EUR 3.95 at December 2027, the value is EUR 35, and the 18-month total return including the EUR 1.90 dividend is about zero. The three-year return is in the high twenties, and almost all of it comes from dividends and earnings recovery rather than re-rating.

6

The balance sheet is the quiet positive, and it is the reason to stand aside and re-enter rather than avoid the stock. Leverage stays at 2.0 to 2.2x net debt to EBITDA (company definition) throughout the unwind. There are no holding-level covenants, floating-rate debt is swapped, and the windfall pays for itself in cash within four to six quarters. The acquisition programme, paused since Q1 2026 while the balance sheet funded inventory, restarts in Q4 2026 (management said so on 5 October) and runs at EUR 55 to 95m a year from 2027. That pace is below the 2030 plan's EUR 100m-plus, but it is enough to add about 3% of revenue and EUR 12 to 16m of EBITA a year from FY28.

7

INDUS's normal business does not compound, so the 2030 targets are a ceiling rather than a base case. Five structural features cap returns: no central purchasing (by policy), no scale benefits shared with customers, 75% of subsidiaries held for over ten years including the weak ones, a tax and interest wedge that absorbs about 45% of each euro of EBITA, and working-capital intensity in the bottom tier of the peer set. The model's FY30 margin of 9.7% and brokers'-basis EPS of EUR 4.64, against targets of 11% and "above EUR 4.50", are a fair reading of what this structure delivers.

8

The plateau branch (about 25% probability) is what would make me wrong on the downside. In the plateau branch, the Western price of ammonium paratungstate (APT, the traded tungsten intermediate) holds near USD 2,500 to 3,000 per metric tonne unit (MTU) through the 2027 contract round. Three forces would hold it there: Chinese raw-material export restrictions persist, the US defence procurement rule from 1 January 2027 bids for traceable supply, and the new Sangdong mine ramps up slowly. BETEK then keeps two-thirds of its price gain, FY27 EPS is about EUR 3.7 to 3.8, the shares hold EUR 35 to 42 through the winter, and management's pattern of low guidance followed by raises restarts in August 2027. The first tests of the plateau branch are Kennametal's results call on 4 November and the Q3 Materials Solutions margin on 12 November (above 20% would support the plateau).

9

A de-rating to EUR 24 to 30 on a visibly repairing balance sheet would make INDUS a long. EUR 24 to 30 is 7.7 to 8.9x normalised EPS of about EUR 3.2 to 3.5. The buy signal needs that price together with three confirmations: the quarterly working-capital and net-debt lines show the release arriving, acquisitions are being announced again, and the initial FY27 guidance range has been set and absorbed. That combination is a cause for concern clearing on a repaired balance sheet in a medium-quality business, and it is the only one of Richard's six investment setups that INDUS can fit in the next 18 months.

The five judgements that move the shares most, with the arithmetic

The sensitivities below use brokers'-basis EPS (after PPA), a 34% tax rate and 24.9m shares, so EUR 1m of adjusted EBITA is worth about EUR 0.027 of EPS.

J1

How much of BETEK's 2026 price gain survives into FY27 (base: half). Materials Solutions revenue rises from EUR 554m in FY25 to about EUR 757m in FY26. About EUR 130m of that increase is price (management says "about two-thirds price"), and the rest is volume: some of it taken from competitors who could not source feedstock, plus the segment's non-tungsten units and small acquisitions. Price earned on inventory bought earlier falls through to profit at roughly 75%. Each 10% of the EUR 130m price gain kept or lost beyond the base is EUR 13m of revenue, about EUR 10m of adjusted EBITA and EUR 0.27 of EPS.

Keeping two-thirds of the price gain (the plateau branch) adds about EUR 17m of EBITA and EUR 0.45 of EPS, taking FY27 EPS to about EUR 3.7 and the segment margin to about 13%. Keeping one-third removes the same amount, taking FY27 EPS to about EUR 2.8 and the segment margin back to its pre-shock 8 to 9%; one-third is the index-linked give-back, which matches the company's statement that BETEK reprices "at short intervals". The 2027 contract round and the Q3 2026 segment margin will narrow this judgement.

J2

Whether INDUS writes down its tungsten inventory (base: a EUR 5m allowance in Q4 2026). Inventories were EUR 557m at June 2026 (EUR 495m at March) and are carried at or near peak feedstock prices. The company has said an abrupt fall in the tungsten price would require valuation allowances, but it has given no threshold or tonnage. A Western APT price below USD 2,000 per MTU before year-end makes an allowance of EUR 15 to 25m more likely than EUR 5m. Each additional EUR 15m costs EUR 0.40 of EPS in the quarter it lands (in FY26 or FY27), has no cash effect, and takes about 0.1x off the leverage ratio's EBITDA denominator.

J1 at its low end and J2 at its high end together make the fast-unwind branch (about 25% probability): FY27 EPS of about EUR 2.5 and net debt to EBITDA briefly at 2.6 to 3.0x. The fast-unwind branch is the configuration in which the market punishes the earnings and ignores the cash.

J3

The tax rate (base 34%; consensus about 29%). FY27 pre-tax profit on the brokers' basis is about EUR 124m: adjusted EBITA of EUR 174m, less PPA amortisation of EUR 22m, less net financial items of EUR 28m. At a 34% tax rate net income is about EUR 82m (EUR 3.30 a share before minorities, EUR 3.24 after); at 29% it is about EUR 88m (EUR 3.49 a share). The five-point difference is worth EUR 0.25 of EPS, a third of my gap to consensus.

The higher rate comes from a structural feature that no broker models: German trade tax is assessed subsidiary by subsidiary, so losses at loss-making partnership subsidiaries cannot be offset against profits elsewhere (EUR 5.98m of tax expense in FY25 and EUR 7.11m in FY24). In a German downturn with more loss-making subsidiaries the rate rises to 36 to 38%, costing another EUR 0.10 to 0.20 of EPS. The FY25 rate of 28.7%, which the sell-side has extrapolated, contained a one-off credit of EUR 8.4m.

J4

The size and timing of the working-capital release (base: EUR 80m in FY27). Working capital on FactSet's definition was 37.9% of trailing revenue at June 2026, against a pre-shock norm of 30 to 33%. The model takes it to 34% at end-2026 and 30.5% at end-2027, and each point of revenue is about EUR 20m of cash. If Western prices hold and working capital stays at 33% at end-2027, FY27 free cash flow is about EUR 130m rather than EUR 182m and net debt is about EUR 620m rather than EUR 571m: about EUR 2 a share of value and EUR 2m of annual interest (EUR 0.05 of EPS). If the unwind is fast and working capital reaches 29%, about EUR 30m more cash arrives alongside the write-down in J2.

The working-capital outcome moves inversely to J1 and J2, because the same tungsten price drives all three. That inverse link is why the enterprise value moves far less than the equity story across the branches.

J5

The multiple applied to normalised earnings (base 8.9x; guideline 14.26x; today about 8.7x). Brokers'-basis 24-month-forward EPS at December 2027 is the mean of FY28 (EUR 3.73) and FY29 (EUR 4.17), about EUR 3.95. Each turn of the multiple is worth EUR 3.95 a share, or 10.7% of today's price. At the ten-year 35th percentile (7.7x) the value is EUR 30; at the median (8.9x) EUR 35; at the 75th percentile (11.4x) EUR 45; at the guideline (14.26x) EUR 56.

The gap between my base multiple and the guideline multiple is worth EUR 21 a share, more than the whole range of FY27 EPS outcomes: J1 to J3 together span about EUR 1.3 of EPS, or EUR 12 a share at 8.9x. The multiple is therefore the largest single judgement in the case, and it is a judgement about the stock's lifecycle phase, which topics #10 and #11 address.

#1 Tailwinds in the operating environment, and headwinds

Score 42

For the two-thirds of INDUS outside BETEK, the environment is slightly better than at any time since 2022; for BETEK, it has flipped from the best possible configuration to the worst.

Evidence. The macro environment has turned up at the margin, the durable positives sit in the Infrastructure and Engineering order books, and the headwinds are specific and mostly dated. The one tailwind that made 2026, Western tungsten scarcity, is already reversing. The table sets out the evidence theme by theme.

Inference and so-what. Outside BETEK, the environment offers low-single-digit volume growth, not an upcycle. The identifiable durable positive is Infrastructure's mandate-driven digital demand, and the identifiable 2027 positive is the German infrastructure fund.

For BETEK, the environment has flipped from the most favourable configuration a non-integrated toolmaker can have to the least favourable. In 2026 BETEK had scarce feedstock that it had pre-financed and absent competitors. From late 2026 it has expensive Western feedstock still in inventory, Chinese finished tools arriving at half its input cost, and integrated rivals following prices down to protect market share. The external change over the next twelve months is therefore large, mostly already reported and skewed to reverse: mildly negative for profit and positive for cash.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side notes include the first-order reversal of the tungsten price and the German macro. None of them includes the Chinese finished-tool channel or BETEK's index-linked repricing mechanics, which together make the FY27 trough deeper and earlier than the stale consensus median implies. I am more constructive than the market narrative on one point: the volume cycle outside BETEK, which the Q2 segment detail supports and which the group headline will hide.

Counter-case, and what would change my view. Western tungsten prices could stay decoupled from Chinese prices if Chinese export licensing stays tight, defence stockpiling absorbs Western material and Sangdong slips. NuWays' view that a "rapid price decline [is] rather unlikely" would then be right for one more year. Three readings would move me toward the plateau branch: a Q3 Materials Solutions margin above 20%, Kennametal reporting a September-quarter timing benefit still above USD 20m on 4 November, or Western APT holding above USD 2,500 per MTU into January.

Score: 42. A shallow volume recovery and one durable niche tailwind sit under a large, policy-made tungsten tailwind that is already reversing, in an interest-rate regime hostile to small leveraged acquirers.

#2 Internally driven corporate change forces, and problems

Score 47

INDUS's internal change is a slow positive drift, and its one bold act, funding BETEK's tungsten supply, was a one-time bet on an external price that consumed the first year of the 2030 plan.

Evidence: leadership and strategy. Leadership is unchanged and extended. CEO Dr Johannes Schmidt (on the board since 2006, CEO since 2018) is contracted to 31 December 2027 and CFO Rudolf Weichert (in post since 2012) to March 2028; there are no named successors, and the Nomination Committee did not meet in FY25. In March 2025 the strategy moved from repair (PARKOUR perform: the automotive exit and the reduction from five segments to three) to growth (EMPOWERING MITTELSTAND). A new compensation system from 2026 ties long-term pay to EBITA growth and a doubling of EPS, with clawbacks and share-ownership guidelines, but it is cash-settled, and insiders hold under 0.05% of the shares.

Evidence: operations. A willingness to sell under-performing subsidiaries was formalised in 2025 and first exercised in October 2026 with MEWESTA (about EUR 5m of sales). Internationalisation is real but small: a shared facility in Grand Rapids for three subsidiaries, AMIRA in Italy, Electro Trading in Sweden and MIKROP in Serbia; international sales are 53% of the total. The operational programmes are specific (63 lean managers, 9 efficiency projects, 6 enterprise resource planning (ERP) system implementations, 14 innovation projects costing EUR 3.3m), but their value in euros is undisclosed. Infrastructure's margin rose from 9.1% to 11.2% in H1 on cost optimisation and mix, which NuWays and Warburg treat as genuine.

Evidence: the supply decision. The one internal act of scale was the Q1 2026 decision to fund BETEK's supply through the tungsten shortage. That decision paid off handsomely in reported profit, and it consumed the balance-sheet capacity that the 2030 plan needed in its first year: deal flow "temporarily decelerated" (NuWays, 8 October).

Inference and so-what. INDUS's internal change is worth low single digits of revenue growth and tens of basis points of margin a year, which is the pace of a competent holding company, not a transformation. The supply decision was a one-time bet on an external variable, not a repeatable improvement in how the group operates.

The next internal positive of any size, the restart of acquisitions, follows the working-capital release rather than preceding it. Management's 5 October statement that it expects further deals before year-end shows that management already sees the balance-sheet pressure easing.

The internal negatives cluster around the same tungsten bet, plus one leadership risk:

  • inventory valuation risk and an H2 margin squeeze at BETEK;
  • Engineering stuck at a 5.6% margin despite record orders;
  • a rising personnel cost ratio (31.9%, heading toward 33% in FY27 as price-led revenue falls away);
  • a CEO term that ends inside the forecast horizon, while the network that sources succession deals rests on the CEO personally.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side treats BETEK's market-share gains as permanent and the pause in acquisitions as a footnote. I expect a third to a half of BETEK's share gain to reverse when small competitors return, and I read the acquisition pause as evidence that the balance sheet cannot fund the 2030 plan and a working-capital shock at the same time. Nobody covering the stock mentions the CEO succession.

Counter-case, and what would change my view. Two events would improve my view. A platform acquisition of EUR 4m-plus of EBITA announced in Q4 2026, alongside a falling working-capital balance, would show the acquisition programme restarting faster than Storskogen or Sdiptech managed after their own pauses. A named CEO successor from inside the deal-sourcing network would remove the 2027 succession question. Both are plausible, and neither is in my numbers before FY28.

Score: 47. Direction better (strategy launched, disposal mechanism live, governance upgraded), resourcing worse (balance sheet fully employed on inventory, acquisitions paused); net close to neutral.

#3 Value chain, industry structure, business model, financial profile, management

Score 42
INDUS has a real but narrowing advantage in buying German family companies cheaply, and no mechanism that compounds returns once it owns them.

Evidence: two markets. INDUS competes in two markets. As an operator, its subsidiaries hold top-three positions in micro-niches (Hauff-Technik in cable entries, MBRAUN in gloveboxes, OFA in compression stockings, and BETEK as global leader in carbide-tipped wear tools for road milling, mining and agriculture), with no customer above 10% of sales and the top ten customers at about 17%. As an acquirer, INDUS buys German succession deals at 5.5 to 6.5x EV/EBIT historically (7 to 7.5x on recent deals), against 8 to 12x paid by private equity, because conservative owners value its promise never to sell.

The acquisition pipeline is demographically secure: the German state development bank KfW counts 125,000 small and medium-sized companies seeking successors each year through 2027. The pipeline is increasingly contested by Lifco (17 German deals since 2018, three of them in 2026), Indutrade and Sdiptech (which has named Germany as its next territory and has SEK 2.4bn available). The operating model forbids central purchasing (33,000 suppliers are managed locally), retains founders and integrates nothing; the holding company has 45 people.

Evidence: financial profile. The model produces mid-pack margins and bottom-tier capital intensity, and EPS has not grown over the cycle: EPS on Viewforth's definition was EUR 3.32 in FY19 and EUR 2.71 in FY25. The reasons are that net interest stepped up from EUR 10 to 16m a year before 2024 to EUR 25 to 28m, and that the tax rate swung between 29% and 43%. The table compares the profile with the compounders that the market re-rates.

Evidence: management. INDUS's managers are competent, honest, long-tenured engineers. They did two decisive things well (the 2023 automotive exit, after a EUR 124m loss in FY22, and the 2026 supply decision), they never overpay, and they set guidance low and raise it within the year. They have also missed every multi-year revenue target: the initial FY23 and FY24 guidance, the legacy target of EUR 2bn of revenue by FY25, and acquired EBITA of EUR 1.9m in FY25 against EUR 8 to 9m targeted. Governance is clean (an unqualified PwC audit opinion, a 100% independent supervisory board, related-party transactions of EUR 832k). Management has no meaningful shareholding: Dr Schmidt owns 6,200 shares, and the employee share plan has been cancelled.

Inference and so-what. INDUS's deal-sourcing advantage is real, moderate and narrowing, and its subsidiaries' niche positions sustain margins of 8 to 10% and no more. The group has no compounding mechanism: each acquisition bought at 6x EBIT into a group earning an 8.5% ROCE leaves the group's return unchanged, and nothing gets cheaper or stickier with scale.

The sector precedents are unambiguous. The compounders that the market re-rates (Lifco, Indutrade, Addtech) have sustained organic growth, incremental returns in the mid-teens or higher, and leverage below 2x; INDUS matches them only on entry discipline. The model should therefore carry no structural margin expansion from competitive advantage, a BETEK quality premium worth a few points of margin in one segment, and acquisition growth only at the pace the balance sheet can fund. The quality that matters most for the next 18 months, balance-sheet discipline, is the one strength the group has demonstrably shown.

Where I differ from the market. NuWays calls the 11% margin target "well within reach"; I treat 11% as the ceiling. The sell-side values INDUS on its 2027 free-cash-flow yield, which is a defensible method, but it applies that yield to a cash figure that includes the one-off working-capital release. The normalised free cash flow of the business is about EUR 110 to 120m a year, about 12% of the market capitalisation, which is fair for an 8.5% ROCE business rather than cheap.

Counter-case, and what would change my view. Active recycling of the portfolio at Sdiptech's pace would lift returns: Sdiptech made eleven disposals and raised its return on capital from 11.9% to 13.2%. INDUS's 2025 disposal policy opens that door, but at 0.3% of sales a year the disposals so far are cosmetic. Central framework agreements for energy and raw materials (Storskogen's model), introduced after the tungsten lesson, would be the first structural change to INDUS's operating model in thirty years.

Score: 42. A durable but contested sourcing advantage over a portfolio of stable, modest-margin, price-taking niches; a mid-pack financial profile with bottom-tier capital intensity; honest, disciplined, non-outlier management.

#4 Conservatism of guidance and the record of delivery and upgrades

Score 48

INDUS's guidance is a reliable floor within the year and no guide to the next year: FY26 guidance will hold or rise, and the first FY27 range in March 2027 will be the negative event.

Evidence. The FY26 guidance of 29 July is for revenue of EUR 1.90 to 2.10bn, adjusted EBITA of EUR 220 to 260m (an 11 to 13% margin), segment margins of 15 to 17% in Materials Solutions, 8.5 to 10.5% in Engineering and 10 to 12% in Infrastructure, and free cash flow of at least break-even. The guidance range implies H2 adjusted EBITA of EUR 96.5 to 136.5m against EUR 123.5m in H1, so even the range already assumes a fade.

The record shows five guidance changes in two years, against a German mid-cap norm of 0.3 to 0.5 a year. The FY26 raises lifted the EBITA midpoint by 45% in four months while cash guidance was cut. The company never guides EPS, tax, interest, PPA amortisation, the price-volume split beyond "about two-thirds price", the contract lag or the inventory timetable. Consensus FY26 sits at the guidance midpoint on EBITA (EBIT of EUR 215m plus PPA) and slightly above it on cash (EUR 32m).

Inference. Management is a tactical sandbagger: it sets initial ranges low, raises them after delivery and cuts them promptly when the environment turns. FY26 guidance will be met, and more likely than not in the upper half of the range. Q3 2026 adjusted EBITA is more likely to come in above my estimate of EUR 59.5m (a Materials Solutions margin of about 17.5%) than below it, for three reasons:

  • Sandvik's Q3 report on 22 October still carried a SEK 104m positive timing benefit, and its customers accepted September price increases;
  • Kennametal's timing benefit is front-loaded into the September and December quarters;
  • Western APT has plateaued rather than fallen.

The fade bites in Q4 2026, through the lag in costs. My probabilities for each guidance event are in the figure below; the most important is a 75% probability that the initial FY27 range in March 2027 is set below the consensus trajectory on earnings (adjusted EBITA of EUR 160 to 195m) and above it on cash.

So-what. Guidance will not be the source of disappointment in FY26; instead, the March 2027 guidance will formalise the FY27 decline that the share price has not priced. The 2030 targets will be reaffirmed rather than raised: the windfall has already lifted EPS above the 2030 EPS target, and the revenue target is out of reach without a deal pace the company has never shown. I put the probability of a quiet re-basing of the 2030 revenue and acquisition targets by 2028 at about 40%; a new CEO's first act often includes a review of targets.

Where I differ from the market. On FY26 I am at the guidance midpoint and the market is marginally above it; the difference is one quarter's timing, and the direction of surprise within the year is upward. For FY27 there is no guidance yet to differ from. My base case is where I expect the range to be set, so the first FY27 guidance event is itself the negative event.

Counter-case, and what would change my view. If management narrows FY26 guidance upward on 12 November and says H2 Materials Solutions margins are holding in the high teens, the plateau branch is live. FY27 guidance in March would then be set at a 9 to 11% margin rather than 8 to 10%, a difference of EUR 15 to 20m of EBITA against my base case.

Score: 48. Within-year guidance is specific, honest and conservative; multi-year delivery has trailed the plan in every environment; the next guidance event is a cut in trajectory that the company has already signposted in words.

#5 Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out and feedback loops

Score 40

INDUS's operating leverage is real and now runs backward: in FY27 a 2% fall in revenue becomes a 27% fall in adjusted EBITA and a 34% fall in EPS.

Evidence: pricing power. BETEK has demonstrated pricing power on a scale almost no industrial company shows: its segment margin rose from 8.1% to 22.4% in H1 2026 (26.9% in Q2) on revenue up 32%, two-thirds of it price, with no volume discounts. Infrastructure has modest pricing power, and Engineering has none (see the three panels below).

The key operating judgementEach 10% of BETEK's 2026 price gain kept or lost is worth about EUR 10m of adjusted EBITA and EUR 0.27 of EPS: keeping two-thirds gives FY27 EPS of about EUR 3.7, and keeping one-third gives about EUR 2.8.

Evidence: operating and financial leverage. Operating leverage is high in both directions. The company's own sensitivity is 1.27% of EPS per 1% of sales at constant margins, and 5.26% of EPS per 50 basis points of margin. In H1 2026 a EUR 92m increase in Materials Solutions revenue produced EUR 61m of EBITA (a 66% drop-through), and in FY20 a 10.6% fall in revenue took EBIT from EUR 118m to EUR 25m. Financial leverage is moderate: net financial debt was EUR 666m at June against a market capitalisation of about EUR 960m, interest cover is 6 to 7x and the interest-rate book is largely fixed or swapped, so a 10% move in enterprise value is a 16 to 17% move in the equity value.

Evidence: cost-out and feedback loops. The scope for cost reduction is small: the reducible cost pool over 18 months is in the low tens of millions of euros against a EUR 1.75bn cost base, wage inflation consumes it in FY27, and it is net positive by EUR 3 to 5m a year thereafter. Four feedback loops are at work:

  • the supply-security loop at BETEK reinforced profits through H1 2026 and is now reversing;
  • the working-capital loop is balancing: it paused the acquisition programme and will restart it;
  • the reputation loop with sellers of family companies is slowly eroding as Nordic acquirers copy INDUS's pitch;
  • the buy-and-hold-forever loop caps returns, because weak subsidiaries are kept.

Inference and so-what. The headline question for this topic is whether revenue growth leads to outsized profit growth, and for FY27 the answer is uncomfortable: the leverage is real and it runs backward. Group revenue falls about 2% (EUR 40m) and adjusted EBITA falls 27% (EUR 64m), a drop-through of about 160%. The drop-through exceeds 100% because the revenue that leaves is price at close to 100% margin, while EUR 17 to 20m of wage inflation lands on a semi-fixed labour base. No cost action changes that arithmetic.

From FY28 the operating leverage turns mildly positive on volume, at the company's normal 20 to 30% drop-through, adding 20 to 40 basis points of margin a year. Financial leverage amplifies the FY27 fall: fixed PPA amortisation and interest turn a 27% EBITA fall into a 33 to 34% EPS fall. No loop in the business converts growth into lower unit costs or stickier customers at group level, which is why the forecasts after FY27 are a drift rather than a growth path.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side's FY27 EBIT margin of 8.7 to 8.8% needs a Materials Solutions margin of 11 to 12%. That margin assumes more of BETEK's pricing power is retained than two pieces of evidence suggest: BETEK's index-linked repricing, and the precedent of Kennametal's Infrastructure business, whose prices adjust downward automatically as APT falls and which lost 360 basis points of gross margin in one quarter in 2019. DNB Carnegie's view that toolmakers "keep most of their price" describes integrated, catalogue-priced toolmakers (Sandvik, Kennametal Metal Cutting), not BETEK.

Counter-case, and what would change my view. Sandvik retained its 2026 price increases, and the large original equipment manufacturers that pushed back in July have since accepted September increases. If BETEK's major customers (Wirtgen and its dealers, and mining fleets running at high utilisation) renew their 2027 framework agreements at 2026 price levels because supply security still outweighs price, the segment margin holds in the mid-teens and J1 resolves at the top of its range. Management's own 5 October language, that tungsten has "peaked for now" while customer relationships are "permanently solidified", is the company's version of that case.

Score: 40. Material two-sided operating leverage now running in reverse on a price the company does not set; moderate financial leverage that amplifies it; little cost-out; no reinforcing loop at group level.

#6 Forecast financials: growth, margins, and scope against the past

Score 35
The model's base case is a windfall year, then a one-third fall in EPS, then a drift in the middle of INDUS's old margin band; double-digit EPS growth appears only as recovery from the FY27 trough.

Against history. The model's growth and margins stay inside INDUS's historical range. From FY21 to FY25 revenue compounded at about 1.5% a year, with negative organic growth in each of the last three years; the model compounds at about 3.3% a year from the FY26 base, or 5 to 5.5% from FY28 (2 to 3% organic volume, 1 to 2% price outside tungsten, 2 to 3% from acquisitions). The FY21 to FY25 margin band of 8 to 10.8% is not exceeded: the 9.3 to 9.7% margin from FY28 is the middle of the old band, not above it.

Brokers'-basis EPS compounds at about 9% a year from FY25 to FY30. One-third of that growth comes from margin recovery to the middle of the band, one-third from acquisitions, and one-third from volume and a lower tax rate (the German corporate tax rate falls a point a year from 2028). Measured from the FY26 peak, however, EPS falls a third and does not regain the peak until FY30. Free cash flow averages about EUR 110m a year over the four years after FY26, similar to the FY23 to FY25 average on FactSet's definition, but its timing is inverted relative to earnings.

Scope for double-digit growth and higher margins than the past. The model's double-digit EPS growth in FY28 (+16%) and FY29 (+10%) is recovery from a trough the market has not yet seen, not growth from a base the market already holds. Margins above the historical band within four years would need three things that the record does not yet show:

  • Engineering sustaining the top of its margin band as it converts its backlog (peer evidence from KION, Krones and Bertrandt says backlogs leak margin);
  • Materials Solutions holding a quality premium of one or two points above its pre-shock margin;
  • acquired companies with EBIT margins above 10% arriving at EUR 75 to 95m of spend a year.

All three together deliver the 2030 target margin of 11%, which is the top of the range of outcomes. The bull case for the drift years, a German capex and construction recovery lifting Engineering to a 10.5% margin and Infrastructure to 12% by FY28, is worth about EUR 16m of EBITA and EUR 0.45 of EPS.

Against consensus. The model's gap to consensus is widest in FY27, and it is a gap in earnings, not revenue. In FY26 the model is in line with consensus on revenue and EBITDA, and brokers'-basis EPS is 7% below on tax and interest. In FY27 revenue is 4% below, EBITDA is about 12% below (EUR 255m against EUR 292m), brokers'-basis EPS is 18% below and free cash flow is about 40% above. Individual FY27 EBITDA forecasts range from Pareto's EUR 247m to Oddo's EUR 310m, with the two recently updated brokers at EUR 263m and EUR 272m. In FY28 revenue and EBITDA are each 4% below consensus, and EPS is 10% below.

Three mechanical items in the model affect how its outputs should be read (EPS before minorities, cash tax charged on pre-PPA profit, and a shift in the Q3 and Q4 2026 quarterly margins); end note 2 explains them. None of them changes an input, and the shifted quarterly margins must not be used as the test for 12 November.

Score: 35. A windfall year, a normalisation year in which EPS falls a third, then a competent drift at the middle of the old margin band with double-digit EPS growth only as recovery from the trough.

From April 2027, a low guidance range, a visible cash release, acquisitions entering estimates as they close, the easier H2 2027 comparison and the 2028 tax cut allow modest upgrades. #9 Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

Score 35
The direction of INDUS's earnings is near-certain and the magnitude is unusually uncertain, but the mechanism is trackable week by week, and every fair-trough value sits below today's share price.

Simplicity of the case. The case is unusually simple in mechanism and unusually concentrated in its driver. One subsidiary, one input price and one policy variable (Chinese export licensing) explain essentially the whole of the FY26 departure from history and the whole of the FY27 return toward it, on both the earnings line and the cash line, because the same inventory generated the margin, consumed the cash and will release it.

That concentration makes the direction near-certain, because no source, including management, expects the premium to persist. It also makes the magnitude unusually uncertain, because the three coefficients that set it are undisclosed: BETEK's repricing interval, its cost-flow lag, and the value and tonnage of its inventory. My estimates of those coefficients are borrowed from Sandvik (a one-month price lag and three-month cost lag in powder; three and nine months in tools) and Kennametal (two quarters of inventory; a quarter of the portfolio index-linked).

The range of outcomes over 18 months. FY27 brokers'-basis EPS ranges from EUR 2.5 to 3.8 around a base of EUR 3.22. The width is about 40% of the base, several times what a 43-company holding normally shows: from FY21 to FY25 adjusted EBITA moved only within EUR 138 to 195m, on volume and mix. The expected value across the three branches is close to the base, so the earnings range is roughly symmetric around the model and negatively skewed only against the stale consensus. The cash range is positively skewed against consensus on every branch except the plateau.

Ordinary risks. Beneath the tungsten mechanism, the ordinary risks of a German industrial holding are moderate and disclosed: a deeper German recession under higher rates (Germany is half of sales; FY20 is the precedent); the failure of a single subsidiary (with Gestalt, IMECO, SMA, Schäfer and Selzer as precedents; EUR 10.5m of goodwill impairment per 10% cut to segment plans; and a pending lawsuit from an insolvency administrator that the company classes as low-to-medium risk); wage inflation; cyber risk; and CEO succession.

Suddenness, predictability and trackability. The tungsten risk could arrive without notice, through one administrative decision in Beijing, but it transmits slowly (two to three quarters through inventory) and is highly trackable through external proxies. INDUS's own disclosure is good at segment level (quarterly segment margins, orders, backlog, working capital on its definition, leverage) and silent on BETEK. The first warning of a faster unwind will therefore come from Kennametal in Pittsburgh or Sandvik in Sandviken rather than from INDUS in Bergisch Gladbach.

The sentiment risk is more probable than the fundamental risk, and faster. A tungsten headline, a read-across from Sandvik or Kennametal, a de-rating on German sentiment, or a Q3 report showing that working capital is not releasing would each hit the shares before any INDUS forecast changed.

Sector and cyclicality precedents. Industrial companies after a raw-material windfall de-rate 30 to 60% from their peak multiple percentile within two to eight quarters, and the share price bottoms at or after the first reported year-on-year earnings decline. The precedents are Kennametal in 2013 (four quarters after the peak margin), Wacker in 2023 (four quarters), Yara in 2023 (to a trough P/E of 6x against an 11x average) and Salzgitter (six quarters, when leverage peaked). During the normalisation these companies are valued on free-cash-flow yield where working capital releases (Sandvik 2012, Kennametal 2015, ArcelorMittal and K+S 2023) and on trough earnings where it does not.

INDUS's first year-on-year EBITA decline is in Q1 2027, reported in May 2027. The precedents put the share-price low between that report and the H1 2027 report, and the cash release is what could make INDUS's de-rating shallower than the precedents.

The fair trough. The downside needs only normalisation, while further upside needs the windfall to persist and the multiple to hold at the top of its range. On normalised brokers'-basis EPS of EUR 3.2 to 3.9, the fair trough value is EUR 21 to 26 at the five-year median multiple of 6.7x, EUR 25 to 30 at the ten-year 35th percentile of 7.7x, and EUR 28 to 35 at the ten-year median of 8.9x. A crash multiple of 5.5x on fast-unwind EPS of EUR 2.5 gives EUR 14. Twelve months ago the shares traded at EUR 20 to 21 on the same business with a weaker balance sheet.

Where I differ from the market. The market's implicit view (targets at EUR 41 to 42, with FY27 cash yield as the anchor) treats the risk as a gentle slope with a floor. I treat it as a two-step decline with a trackable timetable and a floor 20 to 35% below the share price.

Counter-case, and what would change my view. If the Q3 working-capital balance comes in below EUR 580m (company definition, against EUR 627m at June), with nine-month free cash flow clearly positive and Materials Solutions still above a 17% margin, the release is front-loaded. The sell-side's "earnings trough, cash peak" framing would then take hold before the earnings cut rather than after it, which would materially shorten the window for a de-rating.

Score: 35. A simple, concentrated, trackable mechanism with a near-certain direction, a wide range of magnitudes set by undisclosed coefficients, a sentiment risk that leads the fundamental one, and a fair trough well below the price; the ordinary risks beneath it are moderate.

The dashboard's reading. The phase rule reads "Reinforcing" from current momentum: a technical rating of A, a sell-side rating of B, two guidance raises and a 69% one-year return.

The "delivering serial acquirer, mechanical EPS upgrader" setup is the 2028 to 2030 aspiration, and it depends on an acquisition programme that has never run at the required pace.

The dashboard's mechanical phase reading and the model's guideline multiple treat INDUS as a mid-cycle compounder in peak delivery, and the sell-side treats it as a stock at fair value after a run. #11 The fair multiple

Score 35
My fair multiple is 8.5 to 9.0x brokers'-basis 24-month-forward earnings, with the ten-year median of 8.9x as the point estimate, 7.7x as the working floor for the next two quarters and 11.4x as a ceiling that needs conditions not in place before 2028.

The guideline. Viewforth's rule sets the fair multiple from the stock's lifecycle phase and its own ten-year range of two-year-forward P/E: 90th percentile 14.3x ("mania"), 75th 11.4x ("defendable"), median 8.9x ("prudent"), 35th 7.7x ("conservative") and 10th 5.5x ("crash"). The Phases page reads INDUS as Reinforcing and gives the model 14.26x, 50% above today's multiple (9.5x on the dashboard's series, 8.7x on the model's, 8.5x on FactSet's five-year series).

Why the guideline multiple is wrong for INDUS, in four steps.

  1. The guideline assumes a repeatable peak; INDUS's peak is a one-off. The guideline places peak delivery high in the range on the premise that the business can repeat it. Here the company itself disowns the peak, and the 24-month-forward EPS at December 2027 to which any multiple applies (about EUR 3.95) is already the normalised figure. The question is therefore what to pay for the normalised earnings of a holding with a 9 to 10% margin, an 8.5% ROCE, 2 to 4% organic growth and 2 to 2.2x leverage, in a rising-rate regime.
  2. INDUS's own history answers that question period by period. The multiple was 13 to 16x in 2016 to 2018, when INDUS was a steady 10%-margin compounder with positive organic growth at zero rates; 9 to 11x in 2019 to 2021; 5 to 7.5x in 2022 to 2025, through the German recession and negative organic growth; and 8 to 9.5x now, on the windfall. The 2017 to 2018 conditions are the only ones in which INDUS earned its 90th-percentile multiple, and nothing in the next 18 months recreates them.
  3. The multiple must be applied to the EPS basis on which its history was measured. That basis is consensus EPS after PPA amortisation. Applying 14.26x to the model's pre-PPA EPS of EUR 5.19 compounds the phase error with a basis error worth about 31%.
  4. On the guideline's own logic, INDUS belongs in the lower half of its range. A stock whose earnings fall a third inside the return window is in the guideline's "stalling or turning up, where forecasts are more uncertain" condition, which points to the lower half of the range, not the top decile. The ten-year median is therefore a generous choice rather than a harsh one; I use it because the balance sheet is sound, the cash release is real and the business is not broken.

What the sell-side does. NuWays values INDUS on an equal weighting of FY27 free-cash-flow yield (with a 7.5% hurdle) and a DCF, shows the stock at 7.5x FY26 and 11.3x FY27 earnings, and puts fair value at EUR 41. The mean target of EUR 42.3 implies about 10.7x consensus FY27 EPS. Those numbers are defensible on consensus earnings; on my earnings they are 13x.

So-what. The multiple is not a source of return from here, and it is the largest source of risk. At 8.9x on EUR 3.95, fair value at December 2027 is about EUR 35, which is 5% below today's price before the dividend. The stock is therefore fairly valued to slightly rich on my base case, materially rich on the fast-unwind branch, and about right on the plateau branch (8.9x on about EUR 4.4 gives EUR 39).

Where I differ from the market. The market, like the guideline, sees a multiple with room to expand. I see a multiple that has already expanded from 6.7x to 8.5x in a year on a one-off, in a regime that the sector digest describes as refusing re-ratings to small leveraged acquirers.

Counter-case, and what would change my view. A visible restart of acquisitions at EUR 75m-plus a year, with organic volume growth positive for four consecutive quarters and the tax rate falling from 2028, is the configuration in which 11.4x becomes defendable; that configuration is a 2028 story. A take-private approach (private transaction multiples of 8 to 12x against a listed 6 to 7x on normalised earnings) would put a floor under the shares rather than justify a higher multiple, and the 69% rally has made such an approach less likely.

Score: 35. The stock trades at the top of its own five-year range and just above its ten-year median on earnings that fall by a third; the guideline multiple belongs to a different phase and a different era; my fair multiple leaves no re-rating to earn.

#13 Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

INDUS is an honest, well-governed, modestly profitable German holding whose economics do not compound, and its share price has capitalised a one-off profit at the top of the stock's own multiple range. The one-off profit comes from a policy-made tungsten scarcity in one subsidiary, BETEK, and INDUS financed it on its own balance sheet.

The next 18 months are the unwinding of that profit, and the balance sheet repairs itself at the same time. Adjusted EBITA falls from about EUR 239m to about EUR 174m and brokers'-basis EPS from EUR 4.85 to EUR 3.22, and consensus is cut in two dated steps. Meanwhile EUR 80m or more of working capital returns as cash, leverage holds at 2.0 to 2.2x, the equity ratio reaches 40%, and acquisitions restart at a pace below the 2030 plan.

The market knows the direction of the decline and has not priced its size. The company and the sell-side will reveal the size between 12 November 2026 and March 2027. The guideline multiple of 14.26x and the model's +99.5% return should not be carried: the fair multiple is the ten-year median of 8.9x, and at that multiple the 18-month return is about zero.

INDUS is a stock to track closely rather than dismiss, because its enterprise value is far more stable than its equity story. The same tungsten price that sets the earnings moves the cash in the opposite direction. A de-rating to the mid-to-high twenties, against a visibly repairing balance sheet, a low initial FY27 range and resumed acquisition announcements, would be a clean cause for concern clearing in a medium-quality business. The three-year return from there would be about 10% a year, plus whatever re-rating a restarted acquisition programme and positive organic growth eventually earn.

The plateau branch is the one way the shares hold their level through the winter. In the plateau branch, Western tungsten prices hold through the 2027 contract round. That branch will be visible first in Kennametal's call on 4 November and in INDUS's Materials Solutions margin and working-capital balance on 12 November.

End notes

1. Earnings bases. The company guides adjusted EBITA, which is before amortisation of acquired intangibles from purchase price allocation (PPA). Consensus EPS and the ten-year history of the multiple are on the brokers' basis: after PPA amortisation and before one-off items. The Financial Analyst's model reports EPS before PPA amortisation and before minorities (FY26 EUR 5.48, FY27 3.88, FY28 4.49, FY29 4.94, FY30 5.44). The same forecasts on the brokers' basis are EUR 4.85, 3.22, 3.73, 4.17 and 4.64, and the memo uses those brokers'-basis figures whenever it compares with consensus or applies a multiple.

2. Model mechanics for the Financial Analyst. None of these three items changes a forecast input. First, the model's EPS is before minorities (about EUR 0.06 to 0.10 a share) as well as before PPA. Second, the model charges 34% tax on pre-PPA profit, so its cash tax is about EUR 7 to 8m a year too high; its free cash flow is understated and its net debt overstated by that amount, which accumulates to about EUR 35m of net debt by FY30. Third, the model's Q3 and Q4 2026 quarterly margins were shifted down 2.9 points to reconcile an H1 actual held on FactSet's operating-EBITDA basis with a full year on the brokers' basis, so those quarterly margins must not be used as the test for 12 November; the test is my quarterly adjusted EBITA path in #4 and #6. I have kept all forecast inputs as they stand: the October evidence pushes Q3 2026 profit up and FY27 BETEK price retention down by similar amounts within the range of outcomes, and the two sets of evidence agree on the central path. Because no input changed, no inputs-changed.md file is written; the Financial Analyst should address these items in the model itself.

3. Sources. The memo rests on the four sets of research answers (22 to 24 October 2026); the three AlphaSense reports written for it (valuation precedents after raw-material windfalls, the tungsten peer read-across to 12 November, and the holder base); the Financial Analyst's model summary after update 1; the forecast inputs; the FactSet financials block (refreshed 22 October); the dashboard data; the peer table; the Phases data; and the valuation history. The instruction's caution about the date of the latest Earnings Review was resolved by the first set of research answers: that review covers the H1 2026 results of 12 August 2026, the period FactSet shows as last reported.

4. Terms. APT is ammonium paratungstate, the traded intermediate form of tungsten; its price is quoted per metric tonne unit (MTU, 10 kg of tungsten trioxide). "Timing benefit" is the profit a toolmaker earns when selling at current prices products made from cheaper feedstock bought earlier.
